newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Shell to close two European blending units.
newsitem.headline: Shell to close two European blending units.

text.p: Royal Dutch/Shell Group said Tuesday it would sell a Swiss oil refinery and close two lubricant plants but analysts said the moves fell short of the steps needed to deal with weak refining profits in Europe.
The British-Dutch oil giant said it would close two lubricant plants in Belgium and the Netherlands as part of a major reorganization of its European refining operations.

It said it would sell its Cressier oil refinery in Switzerland, but keep its options open on the Berre l'Etang refinery in southern France, where workers went on strike Tuesday due to industry-wide cutbacks.

It also announced a major cost-cutting drive in its European administrative operation, which could yield as much savings as the refinery measures, said Paul Skinner, a director of Shell International Petroleum.
Analysts said the measures fell short of what was needed.

"It's not exactly a radical ruthless restructuring of their European downstream business," said Alan Marshall, oil analyst at Robert Fleming Securities, referring to refining and marketing as opposed to "upstream" exploration and production.

Shell's announcement follows more drastic moves in Europe by other companies in refining. For example, British Petroleum Co. Plc and Mobil Corp. in August won approval for a plan to pool $5 billion in European marketing and refining assets.
"Compared to the BP/Mobil merger, this is pretty tame given that Shell's exposure to refining is bigger than theirs, Marshall said.

Skinner said the moves addressed the problem of low profits at the weakest of Shell's 14 European refineries. Shell's strong share of the European refining market has hindered its efforts to form an alliance or a merger with another company and negotiations in that area had failed, he added.

"We have not had success and that has been a little bit disappointing and frustrating," Skinner told reporters. "But if we seem to be doing it unit by unit, I don't think you should preclude the possibility that at some stage a more wide-ranging rationalisation might be a possibility."
He said the root of the problem was 10 percent excess refining capacity in Europe and noted Europe exports about 5 billion gallons of gasoline a year.
European refining margins have been $1.50 to $2 a barrel of oil in recent years, he said, adding he did not expect a big improvement soon.
He said he hoped to announce a definitive policy towards the Berre l'Etang refinery, which employs 400 people, in January.
